Philemon — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Philemon lived in Colossae. Henry describes him as a man of some wealth and standing who had come to faith through Paul's ministry.

Onesimus was enslaved to Philemon. He had fled, reached Rome and there became a Christian through Paul's preaching.

Henry understands Paul to have kept Onesimus with him long enough to see evidence of genuine conversion.

Onesimus wanted to repair the harm done through his departure, yet feared the punishment that could follow. He therefore asked Paul to write on his behalf.

Henry praises Paul's letter as particularly compelling and beautiful in its reasoning and appeals.

Paul's joy in Philemon's love (verses 1–7)

Faith in Christ and love for him should unite believers more closely than outward family or social ties.

Paul remembered his friends individually in private prayer. We should also bring Christian friends before God regularly, thinking about what they need and carrying them in our hearts.

Differences of opinion or practice in nonessential matters should not destroy affection between believers faithful to the truth.

Paul wanted to know whether his friends' faith and love were real, growing and fruitful.

Philemon's good deeds comforted and encouraged him and others. They therefore desired that he would continue increasing in these fruits for God's glory.

Paul's loving appeal for Onesimus (verses 8–14)

It does not diminish our dignity to ask humbly, even when we could demand something as a matter of authority.

Paul chose to appeal through love rather than command on behalf of the man converted through his ministry, Onesimus.

The name Onesimus means “useful.” Formerly he had been unprofitable to Philemon, but conversion had made him useful.

Those living without holiness do not fulfill the highest purpose of their existence.

What a wonderful change conversion brings: turning evil into good and the formerly unprofitable into useful people!

Henry describes religious servants as a treasure to a household because they conscientiously use their time and fulfill their trusts.

Yet opportunities for useful service elsewhere should not lead anyone to ignore genuine obligations. A key sign of repentance is a desire to fulfill duties formerly neglected.

In Henry's reading of the events, Onesimus acknowledged his wrongdoing in leaving and now wished to make amends.

We often do not know what providential purposes God will accomplish through changes of place or plans originally undertaken for wrong reasons.

Without God's overruling mercy, some of our own sinful plans would have led us to ruin.

Receive a repentant brother and forgive the debt (verses 15–22)

We must never minimize the evil of sin itself. But when dealing with a repentant sinner, we should follow God's merciful example and cover the offense rather than keep holding it against the person.

People changed by grace can become blessings to those around them.

Christianity does not abolish genuine obligations toward others; it guides us in fulfilling them rightly.

Repentant people should openly acknowledge harm done to others. Henry understands Onesimus to have admitted his fault to Paul.

Fellowship between Christians does not erase distinctions of property.

Paul's proposal that another person's debt should be charged to him voluntarily illustrates one person accepting another's obligation to free that person from a deserved penalty.

Henry sees this as a figure of Christ willingly bearing the punishment of our sins, so that we may receive his righteousness.

Although Philemon was Paul's spiritual son, Paul appealed to him as a brother.

And although Onesimus was a poor enslaved man, Paul pleaded for him as earnestly as if asking a great personal favor.

Christians should bring one another joy and encouragement. People can expect trouble from the world, but should find consolation among other believers.

When comforts disappear, trust the Lord, use the available means and persevere in prayer. Prayer is powerful, but it does not earn what God grants.

Believers who never meet again on earth will soon meet before God's throne to praise his redeeming love.

Onesimus's conversion should encourage the most deeply guilty sinners to seek God. It must never become an excuse for postponing repentance: many die in their sins, and hardening the heart against present conviction is dangerous.

Paul's greetings and blessing (verses 23–25)

Believers may find especially great enjoyment of God's presence when suffering together for Christ.

Grace is the finest blessing we can wish for ourselves or others. Paul began and ended his letter with it.

All grace comes from Jesus Christ, who purchased and gives it.

If his grace is with our spirits, what more do we need for true happiness?

Let us learn now to value what people often recognize only when dying: even the smallest portion of genuine grace and faith is worth more than an earthly kingdom.
classic_reading:
Philemon was an inhabitant of Colosse, a person of some note and wealth, and a convert under the ministry of St. Paul. Onesimus was the slave of Philemon: having run away from his master, he went to Rome, where he was converted to the Christian faith, by the word as set forth by Paul, who kept him till his conduct proved the truth and sincerity of his conversion. He wished to repair the injury he had done to his master, but fearing the punishment his offence deserved might be inflicted, he entreated the apostle to write to Philemon. And St. Paul seems no where to reason more beautifully, or to entreat more forcibly, than in this epistle.
[Phlm.1.1-Phlm.1.7]
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle's joy and praise for Philemon's steady faith in the Lord Jesus, and love to all the saints. | (1-7) |
He recommends Onesimus as one who would make rich amends for the misconduct of which he had been guilty; and on behalf of whom the apostle promises to make up any loss Philemon had sustained. | (8-22) |
Salutations and a blessing. | (23-25) |
Verses 1-7
Faith in Christ, and love to him, should unite saints more closely than any outward relation can unite the people of the world. Paul in his private prayers was particular in remembering his friends. We must remember Christian friends much and often, as their cases may need, bearing them in our thoughts, and upon our hearts, before our God. Different sentiments and ways in what is not essential, must not make difference of affection, as to the truth. He inquired concerning his friends, as to the truth, growth, and fruitfulness of their graces, their faith in Christ, and love to him, and to all the saints. The good which Philemon did, was matter of joy and comfort to him and others, who therefore desired that he would continue and abound in good fruits, more and more, to God's honour.
[Phlm.1.8-Phlm.1.14]
Verses 8-14
It does not lower any one to condescend, and sometimes even to beseech, where, in strictness of right, we might command: the apostle argues from love, rather than authority, in behalf of one converted through his means; and this was Onesimus. In allusion to that name, which signifies "profitable," the apostle allows that in time past he had been unprofitable to Philemon, but hastens to mention the change by which he had become profitable. Unholy persons are unprofitable; they answer not the great end of their being. But what happy changes conversion makes! of evil, good; of unprofitable, useful. Religious servants are treasures in a family. Such will make conscience of their time and trusts, and manage all they can for the best. No prospect of usefulness should lead any to neglect their obligations, or to fail in obedience to superiors. One great evidence of true repentance consists in returning to practise the duties which have been neglected. In his unconverted state, Onesimus had withdrawn, to his master's injury; but now he had seen his sin and repented, he was willing and desirous to return to his duty. Little do men know for what purposes the Lord leaves some to change their situations, or engage in undertakings, perhaps from evil motives. Had not the Lord overruled some of our ungodly projects, we may reflect upon cases, in which our destruction must have been sure.
[Phlm.1.15-Phlm.1.22]
Verses 15-22
When we speak of the nature of any sin or offence against God, the evil of it is not to be lessened; but in a penitent sinner, as God covers it, so must we. Such changed characters often become a blessing to all among whom they reside. Christianity does not do away our duties to others, but directs to the right doing of them. True penitents will be open in owning their faults, as doubtless Onesimus had been to Paul, upon his being awakened and brought to repentance; especially in cases of injury done to others. The communion of saints does not destroy distinction of property. This passage is an instance of that being imputed to one, which is contracted by another; and of one becoming answerable for another, by a voluntary engagement, that he might be freed from the punishment due to his crimes, according to the doctrine that Christ of his own will bore the punishment of our sins, that we might receive the reward of his righteousness. Philemon was Paul's son in the faith, yet he entreated him as a brother. Onesimus was a poor slave, yet Paul besought for him as if seeking some great thing for himself. Christians should do what may give joy to the hearts of one another. From the world they expect trouble; they should find comfort and joy in one another. When any of our mercies are taken away, our trust and hope must be in God. We must diligently use the means, and if no other should be at hand, abound in prayer. Yet, though prayer prevails, it does not merit the things obtained. And if Christians do not meet on earth, still the grace of the Lord Jesus will be with their spirits, and they will soon meet before the throne to join for ever in admiring the riches of redeeming love. The example of Onesimus may encourage the vilest sinners to return to God, but it is shamefully prevented, if any are made bold thereby to persist in evil courses. Are not many taken away in their sins, while others become more hardened? Resist not present convictions, lest they return no more.
[Phlm.1.23-Phlm.1.25]
Verses 23-25
Never have believers found more enjoyment of God, than when suffering together for him. Grace is the best wish for ourselves and others; with this the apostle begins and ends. All grace is from Christ; he purchased, and he bestows it. What need we more to make us happy, than to have the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ with our spirit? Let us do that now, which we should do at the last breath. Then men are ready to renounce the world, and to prefer the least portion of grace and faith before a kingdom.
